Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: What do you think the internal reaction is in Russia to the news that Ryan Evans, a Reuters safety advisor, was killed in Ukraine?
Answer: I read some posts from pro-Russian bloggers claiming that the Sapphire Hotel in Kramatorsk, where Ryan was killed, was a rallying point for "hundreds of foreign mercenaries” but this is, of course, rubbish. I've been to Kramatorsk many times, and I know the part of the city where the hotel is located. Since it's not too far from the frontline, Kramatorsk is full of soldiers and is often a target of Russian missile strikes (the air raid alert in this city rarely goes off). I don't believe this hotel was a legitimate target (it was a civilian object), but this has never stopped the Russians from launching a missile. Ryan Evans, the Reuters security advisor who was killed yesterday. (Picture: Ryan Evans) Ryan Evans, the security advisor for the Reuters journalists and a former British soldier, should have known this. Additionally, the hotel is very close to the city center, which has been a preferred target of Russian missile strikes in the past. The “Ria Lounge” pizzeria, where 13 people were killed in 2023, many of them journalists, is just around the corner. I feel sorry for Mr. Evans and the people who were injured during this attack, but they were in a place you would be better off avoiding. The cheap guest houses on the outskirts of Kramatorsk may not have air conditioning or a swimming pool, but the chances of being surprised by a Russian missile in your sleep are much lower there.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: How do soldiers know if they are in the front line?
Answer: If, for whatever reason, you haven't figured it out on your own, other soldiers will tell you that you’ve reached the zero line (the line closest to the enemy). It’s practically impossible not to be aware of where the frontline is. In Ukraine, many things you do are directly influenced by your distance to the frontline. If you come within a few kilometers, you need an armored vehicle with a jammer; otherwise, you’ll fall victim to a Russian drone. Near the frontline in Donetsk. (Picture by the author of this post) There will also be restrictions on the use of GPS, light discipline at night, extended curfews, and other measures. Soldiers at numerous checkpoints will tell you what you can do and what is forbidden. Additionally, roads leading directly to the frontline are closed to civilian traffic. Last but not least, you can often hear (and sometimes even see) the fighting: artillery explosions, FABs (Russian gliding bombs that make a lot of noise), and, if you get really close, machine guns and other infantry weapons.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Why is Ukraine killing their own people who try to escape serving in the military?
Answer: Unless they are fighting for the Russian Army, Ukraine is not killing any of its citizens. What happens is that some of our draft dodgers are taking huge risks when they try to cross the border illegally. For example, if you attempt to swim across the treacherous and fast currents of the Tisa River to make it to Romania, you can only blame yourself if you drown. The river of death: the Tisa River between Ukraine and Romania. (Picture: State Border Guard Service of Ukraine) The same goes for those daredevils who try to cross the Carpathian mountain border at night and in bad weather. No sane mountaineer would do such a thing. I don't blame anyone who tries to avoid military service in Ukraine. The chances of being killed on the frontline are not low. However, we also should be fair. You cannot blame the Ukrainian authorities for implementing the laws the parliament has voted for.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: We know the news is lying about almost every aspect about the war in Ukraine. But why is this happening?
Answer: I don't see where the news is lying, except in Russia. Most Western news organizations provide a good picture of what's happening on the ground in Ukraine. They often make errors when they try to predict the future, but we need to differentiate between news, analysis, and opinion. The people who really spread a lot of nonsense are the pro-Ukraine and pro-Russia folks on social media, including some Ukrainian bloggers (who should know better). What they post is often one-sided propaganda and nonsense. The reasons for this are pretty clear: Surprisingly, in Ukraine, it's the other way around. People are hungry for truthful and unbiased information. They want to know what's really going on, not read something that turns out to be untrue within twenty-four hours. When your life (or that of your relatives and friends) depends on it, trusting the wrong information can be fatal.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Isn't it perfectly obvious that the Ukrainian incursion into Kursk, like previous incursions, has failed miserably? The Russians have controlled it without slowing their steady conquests in Ukraine itself. Ukrainian forces now risk annihilation.
Answer: This question, although poorly worded, deserves some merit. Ukraine's recent incursion into the territory of the Russian Federation had several objectives, and not all of them have been met (yet). The primary (and most important) goal of the Armed Forces of Ukraine was to successfully execute this operation. They took the Russian defenders by surprise and gained a relatively large area (around 1,000 square kilometers) in just a few days. In this regard, the operation was a complete success. It was certainly much more successful than the botched Russian operation north of Kharkiv earlier this summer. During a supply trip to Donetsk. Ukraine is not only holding the ground it has seized in the Kursk oblast, but they are (albeit slowly) taking more of it. One might have thought that after more than two weeks of Ukrainian troops being present on their territory, the Russians would be able to slowly push them back, but this hasn't happened. Russia seems to be having enormous problems containing the Ukrainian operations. Ukraine expected that Russia would have to divert some of its combat units in Donetsk to fight the Ukrainian invaders in Kursk, but this has only happened on a very limited scale. It is estimated that not more than 5,000 Russian troops have moved from the eastern frontline to Kursk. Meanwhile, Russian combat operations in Donetsk were not significantly affected by this redeployment and continue. The strategically important city of Pokrovsk is at risk of being taken by the Russians. In this regard, the results of the Ukrainian operation are somewhat mixed. I think it’s still too early to say whether it was a success or a failure. What is safe to say, on the other hand, is that Ukrainian forces do not “risk annihilation,” neither in Kursk, nor in Donetsk, nor elsewhere.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: What is the best way to travel between Lviv and Kiev, Ukraine by train or bus?
Answer: I make the trip pretty often and the best way to travel is probably by train. If you take an intercity train, you can make the trip in six and a half hours. On the downside, train tickets are sometimes hard to come by (they are quickly sold out). The train is also more expensive than the bus, especially if you travel 1st class. Another problem is that there aren't that many (good) connections. You have about ten trains every day on this route and many of them depart from Kyiv (or Lviv) in the early morning hours. At the (old) bus station in Kyiv. If you're sensitive to bad smells, you shouldn't go there. Traveling by car can be quicker (depending on traffic) and, if you share the expenses with other travelers, it's also cheaper. On the other hand, the roads aren't that good and I find driving from Kyiv to Lviv always quite tiresome. Last but not least, there's the bus. It’s the cheapest way to get from Kyiv to Lviv, but also the slowest. Most buses stop many times to pick up travelers. The comfort is also rather meh. The bus drivers do not let you use the toilet on the bus because they are too lazy to clean it. In addition, not every bus has air conditioning and punctuality is also not their strongest point. The biggest problem, at least for foreigners, however, is the constant change of itineraries. Five minutes prior to departure, you get a phone call from the bus company that you should take bus B instead of A. Of course, nobody speaks English. What I like about the buses, on the other hand is that there are so many connections. You can go to the bus station without a ticket and just take the next bus that goes in your direction and pay the driver in cash.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: How does the military feel when they are sometimes portrayed as idiots in movies?
Answer: My buddies and I always took it with humor and even embraced it. When I was a paratrooper in the German Army, “Now Where Did the 7th Company Get to?” was our most beloved movie. In this French comedy, they really took the pi** out of every soldier, especially the Germans. We never had a problem with it. When you serve in a good unit, you are above these things. Scene from the movie “Mais où est donc passée la 7ème compagnie” (“Now Where Did the 7th Company Get to?” from 1973. (Picture: Gaumont) Once during a large maneuver on a German Army training ground, our company sergeant major invited all of us NCOs (non-commissioned officers) to the local pub in a small village. Of course, we started to get drunk immediately. One of us found a song in the jukebox that we decided to play endlessly: “Ich bin beim Bund, ich bin ja so in armer Hund!” (I’m in the German army, I am such a poor dog!) by the great German singer Udo Lindenberg. The song makes fun of the army and is even a bit insulting. Our sergeant major, who was (and still is) a man without humor, was getting pretty angry when he heard the lyrics but there was nothing he could do about it. We didn't violate any regulations. So the song played on and on, the sergeant major’s face got redder and redder, and we all had a good time.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Have you ever been declared missing or dead?
Answer: Twice. Both times I was declared dead. The first time was during the Bosnian War when I ended up in a prisoner-of-war camp for several weeks. I had left my passport in a hotel and when the hotel staff alarmed the authorities about my disappearance, they assumed that I must have been killed. This was a logical assumption given the circumstances: Srebrenica had just fallen into the hands of the Serbs and thousands of Bosnians were being murdered in the mountains and forests around the city. After my release from the POW camp, I went to the German consulate in Split, Croatia, to report that I had lost my passport and the clerk there just said: “Ah, there you are, we all thought you were dead!” The location where I've been wounded. (Picture by the author of this post) The second time was earlier this year in Donetsk, Eastern Ukraine. After I had barely survived an artillery attack where two of my friends had been killed, one of the Ukrainians reported back to our office/warehouse that I was “200” (the military code for Killed in Action), when in fact I was “300” (Wounded in action). For a moment, my coworkers in the office were shocked, but fortunately, the mistake was quickly corrected.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: What is the significance of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Ukraine for India-Ukraine relations?
Answer: It’s in India’s best interest to maintain good relations with Ukraine. Ukraine and Poland (which Modi visited yesterday) have become important players on the international stage. Additionally, angering Ukraine would mean alienating the entire West, something India cannot afford. Modi’s visit also signals a small but noticeable shift away from Moscow. India still has strong economic and military ties to the Kremlin (a significant portion of India’s military hardware comes from Russia), but Russia has lost influence on the international stage. There were many Indians this morning in Kyiv. They were here to welcome their Prime Minister in a very relaxed and friendly atmosphere. (Picture by the author of this post) The war in Ukraine has revealed that our (and India’s) perception of Russia has been highly inaccurate. Russia isn’t the superpower we once believed it to be but rather a corrupt and nearly bankrupt kleptocracy that produces low-quality weapons and where nothing works properly. Such a failed state is certainly not the best partner for a rising industrial superpower like India. Modi’s visit sends a signal to Putin (whom he met in July): We don’t need you; we can work with anyone.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: How much of a difference are the 16,000+ US veterans and others who've signed up to help fight on the side of Ukraine making in the Russia-Ukraine War?
Answer: I think 500+ US veterans fighting in the Armed Forces of Ukraine is a more accurate number. Rest assured, however, they do make a difference. Every single foreign volunteer makes a difference. When I fought for the guerrillas in Kosovo, we were only two foreign volunteers in our zone of operations (an area held by a division-sized number of troops). People told me after the war that when we arrived, it gave an enormous boost to their morale: “The world hasn't forgotten us, there are two Germans here!” Just the fact that foreigners are willing to give their lives for the freedom of your country is incredibly important. In addition, most of the US veterans in Ukraine possess useful skills. They are already familiar with many of the weapons that the United States has delivered to Ukraine. A group of former US Marines in Ukraine. It’s also good to have a few soldiers with additional skill sets with you. If you encounter a problem on the battlefield and the Ukrainian way of doing things doesn't work, you can always try the American way. When I visit frontline troops in eastern Ukraine, the soldiers and officers always ask me hundreds of questions: “How did you do this and that in the German Army?” I think these exchanges of experience and knowledge are extremely fruitful. Due to the influence of foreign fighters, instructors, and advisors (not all of them Americans), many things have changed in the way the Ukrainians conduct war. The positive impact of these individuals cannot be overstated.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: What is a serious enough reason for you to join the war, to leave your home and children?
Answer: The answer is already in your question. You join the war to defend your home and your loved ones. You fight so that your children have a future. If you have no family, then you fight for your friends—for the right to live your life the way you want, for your freedom, and for the freedom of others. You fight to protect the weak against the strong, to help in the fight against the invaders. These are all good and noble reasons to pick up a weapon and fight. True heroes: Russian volunteers who are fighting on the side of Ukraine during an incursion into Belgorod, Russia, earlier last year. On the other hand, “Claiming your nation’s historic rights,” “Doing God’s will,” “Fighting for the greatness of your country,” fighting for a flag, a bunch of politicians, or against another ethnic or religious group “because they are different,” are pretty bullsh*t reasons to lose your life for.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: How do you tell if a soldier has been in combat?
Answer: In Ukraine, you go to a city where a combat unit has its barracks and compare the soldiers there to the “posers” in Kyiv. You’ll immediately spot the differences: A combat medic from a unit we support near the frontline. And, last but not least: Wartime injuries. Sadly, most combat soldiers get to see the cities only after they’ve been injured on the battlefield. Many soldiers have bandages and casts and make use of a walking stick or even a wheelchair.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: How well-trained is the Ukrainian Army?
Answer: The Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) lack personnel and funds and this also impacts the quality of their training: Ukrainian soldiers during training on an AGS-17 multiple grenade launcher. What Western recruits learn in several weeks is often taught in just a few days. Of course, the quality of the training suffers. (Picture: Scott Peterson) Unfortunately, the situation isn’t getting better. Almost all of the new soldiers are now conscripts who require more training time than a (usually highly motivated and prepared) volunteer. Many combat units offer additional training courses near the frontline but this isn't sufficient.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Do people actually believe that Ukraine is winning?
Answer: I believe that Ukraine will win this war. What makes me optimistic is my experience from two previous wars, Bosnia and Kosovo. Both times, a much weaker country was attacked by its big and aggressive neighbor (Serbia). When the Serbs started murdering civilians in Kosovo, we didn’t even have an army. Despite these disadvantages, in both wars good prevailed against evil. It took a long time, though. For many months and years, nobody would have thought that David may have a chance against Goliath. Especially the International Press was very much of the opinion that fighting the mighty Serbian army was futile and as good as suicide. Picture by the author of this post. What changed the outcome was the intervention of the free world. NATO and its allies decided that enough (genocide and murder) was enough and began supporting the people of Bosnia. Later on, they did the same in Kosovo. Once NATO became more active, the wars didn't last much longer. The Serbian forces in Bosnia suffered major defeats in three consecutive battles and the war ended. In Kosovo, it took NATO 78 days to bomb the Serbs out of the country. Lessons learned: The Russians have yet to understand this.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: How do you think the families of foreign military volunteers are coping with their deaths in Ukraine?
Answer: I spoke with several relatives of foreign fighters who were killed in Ukraine. What surprised me the most was how composed they were. I dealt with grieving relatives of soldiers in other wars (Bosnia and Kosovo) and unfortunately, things can sometimes turn ugly: We had family members accusing us of having killed their sons/brothers, or at least of being responsible for their deaths. We even had the grandfather of one of our soldiers in Kosovo talking to a prosecutor about it. Fortunately, I never heard of similar stories in Ukraine. All the family members and friends of the deceased I talked to were reasonable and cooperative. Without any exception, all of them wanted to know more about the circumstances of how their loved ones died. The Armed Forces of Ukraine can be very tight-lipped in this regard. The best thing to do in such a case is to connect them with one (or several) military unit members of the dead soldier. This has always worked very well. Although these cases are very sad and heartbreaking, most relatives are coping well with the situation. They all knew that something like this could eventually happen. Every foreign volunteer who signs up for the Armed Forces of Ukraine (and their family members, as well) should be aware that not every foreign fighter survives the war. Death should not come as a surprise and everyone should be prepared for it.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Who is the greatest hero of the current Ukraine war?
Answer: The soldiers of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU), especially those in the assault units. This does not include their officers, especially not the generals and the battalion and brigade commanders, who are often of questionable value. While the AFU has some competent squad, platoon, and company leaders, as you move up the ranks, you quickly become disappointed. After 904 days of the most brutal fighting against a superior enemy, we can thank the men and women of the AFU that the Russians aren’t standing on the border to Poland. In the company of true heroes. They may not look like it, especially when your only idea of how a hero should look comes from Hollywood movies, but these folks are the real deal. Sure, the president and some other government officials played an important role (at least at the beginning), but it’s the soldiers who are bearing the brunt of the fight, making the greatest sacrifices. In Ukraine, they say, “Every day has a new hero,” but this hero is always an ordinary soldier.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Which type of stolen valor is more prevalent, non-soldiers pretending they are soldiers, or soldiers pretending they’re more important or heroic than they are?
Answer: Soldiers exaggerating or lying about their service time is extremely common, even among foreign volunteers in Ukraine. I know people who've been in the war for less than ten days (and then f*cked off because they couldn't handle it) and now, they won't shut up about it. Their social media profiles look like the pages of a freaking war museum. Then there are the zillions of special forces soldiers here and the “my unit, we were some kind of penal battalion” idiots. Still, I prefer all of these freaks over the ‘I- cannot-tell-you-which- unit-I was-in-because-it’s-confidential” fellows. They are the peak of the ‘stolen valor” iceberg. The former logistics guy suddenly becomes infantry overnight and when you point it out to them (which I occasionally do), they get angry. Of course, there are also people here who never served and have invented a military career but it is pretty easy to discover their lies, they aren't very good at it. The embellishers, on the other hand, are much more difficult to spot. Their lies are built on some facts and as long as you don't know anyone who has served with them in the same unit or send them to a training course (where they all fail), chances are good that they get through with their bull.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: How far is Ukraine being benefited by the fundraising campaigns going on in the internet?
Answer: I don't know many Ukrainians who are not involved in fundraising activities to support the war effort. Unlike the big organizations, however, these “micro-fundraisers” have relatively modest (but at the same time very concrete) aims. Nobody wants to raise millions but they need USD 500 for a new reconnaissance drone for a particular army unit or (what often happens) smaller sums of money for car spare parts. Unfortunately, the army’s budget isn't big enough to cover all these costs, and more often than not, the soldiers have to pay for these items from their salary. Just imagine a US Marine having to pay the repairs for his Humvee! I think these small fundraisers are very effective. A group of soldiers needs a particular item, people donate money (because they’re relatively small, the sums come together pretty fast), and the article is bought and immediately shipped to the frontline. A soldier from an “Azov” unit with night vision devices we sent to his unit. If you want to support us, send me an email (address in my profile description). No military in the world has a faster and more efficient procurement organization than our Ukrainian micro fundraisers. No administration costs, no delays, and, most importantly, the soldiers get what they need and not some useless crap. There is also as good as zero misuse as the money is mostly raised in private circles. People who donate most often know the person they give the money to. Usually, they also know the soldiers who will benefit from the donation. I cannot say much about the big organizations (as I mostly stay away from them) but these Ukrainian individuals have my fullest respect.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: What's it like for soldiers to be in a firefight?
Answer: Everything depends on who fires first. If it’s your side, you’ll have an enormous advantage: On the shooting range in Ukraine. Extensive training and drills are of utmost importance for surviving a firefight. (Picture by the author of this post) On the other hand, if the enemy surprises you with an attack, the situation looks very different: If your unit is inexperienced, there’s a risk of panic breaking out, leading to soldiers fleeing the battlefield. However, if you’re with well-trained soldiers, you’ll be able to respond effectively to the situation, for example, by returning fire, flanking maneuvers, evasive actions, or even a counterattack.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Do you believe that Ukraine's incursion into western Russia is a distraction or a strategic move?
Answer: It's a strategic move with enormous risks involved. This much can be said after more than a week of fighting inside the territory of the Russian Federation. Ukraine has announced that it will commit additional troops to this operation to keep momentum. To me, it appears as if the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine is trying to force the Russians into making a decision: either continue their offensive operations in Donetsk (and risk losing even more territory in the Kursk and neighboring oblasts) or concentrate their main efforts on the defense of their homeland. The thinking goes that Russia doesn't have enough troops to do both. This is highly risky for several reasons: That the Ukrainians have decided to pursue this path despite these risks (it is said that the former head of the AFU, General Zalushnyy, had rejected all plans for such an operation) could mean two things: Time will tell. Until now, the operation has been extremely successful. The most important “ingredient“ of every attack, the element of surprise, had been preserved which allowed the Ukrainian troops to completely overrun the (few and disorganized) Russian defenders. Tactical maneuvers were executed with swiftness and often with brilliance. Let's cross our fingers that the AFU will continue this way and achieve their goals.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: What do you know about the military commandant’s office that Ukraine set up in occupied Kursk?
Answer: This piece of news reminds me of an episode from the Bosnian War. One day, the Croats were inaugurating a post office in our small frontline city. Some politicians were cutting a ribbon in front of the state TV cameras. I learned about it while I was watching the evening news. The next day, I went there to send a few letters home and make a phone call to my girlfriend in Germany. When I arrived at the post office, the main entry was closed. I found a small side door that was open and entered the building. A completely bored post worker told me that no, I couldn't make any phone calls from there and it also wasn't possible to send or receive any letters. I went back to my buddies who had a good laugh. The next time I went on leave, I traveled to Imotski, Croatia, which was more than fifty kilometers away from the frontline, and sent my letters from there.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: As a soldier, have you ever accidentally killed an innocent civilian?
Answer: Two peasants drove with their tractor over an anti-tank mine which I had placed there earlier. This happened in Kosovo during the time of the NATO airstrikes. There was a lot of fighting on the ground, especially in our area, but to my surprise, there were still some civilians around. We suspected that at least some of these folks were Serbian spies, but we couldn’t prove it. After an enemy offensive, my guerrilla unit had to withdraw to the mountains. Before we left, we mined all the approach routes the enemy could use. Whenever we encountered a farmer, we informed them about the mines so they could avoid getting hurt. Three days later, after the enemy offensive had ended, we returned to “our” valley” to remove the mines. Some of our devices had killed enemy soldiers, while others were duds, but when I arrived at a small road crossing where we had placed two anti-tank mines, I found an overturned and badly damaged tractor. In Kosovo, during the time of this incident. While looking for the second mine (the first one had been activated by the tractor), a peasant from a nearby village approached us and told us that two of his neighbors had been killed when their tractor drove over the mine. He pointed to a spot nearby where I could see a shoe covered in blood. We didn't tell him who had planted the mines. I didn't see any point in doing so. These people came from a village that (to my best knowledge) had never supported the guerrilla. And the fact that this guy had been around while our enemy was in the area made him double suspicious. I never thought twice about this incident, and I never felt bad about it. In war, sh*t happens.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Is Ukraine really winning the war against the Russians?
Answer: Let’s be realistic. At the moment, both sides are far away from anything you could call a victory. If we, the Ukraine supporters, take off our rose-colored glasses and take a look at the map, we can see that the frontline is extremely fragile in the Pokrovsk direction. The Russian forces are advancing towards Myrnohrad which may soon enable them to interrupt an extremely important Ukrainian logistics route. Not good! There are other smaller Russian advances in other frontline sectors but this one is the most threatening. In addition, Ukrainian forces are still lacking personnel. Of course, the Kursk operation has brought us new hope (together with the introduction of the F-16 fighter aircraft) but it’s still too early to think about the impact this operation may have on the overall situation. Right now, it has more of a moral and political effect and not so much a military/strategic one, and it’s also still unclear whether it will be a success or a complete failure. On the road in Donetsk (Picture by the author of this post) The Russians have at least an equal number of serious problems. Atrocious leadership, low morale, and lack of modern equipment are only a few of them. While the Ukrainian forces have demonstrated that they are extremely resilient and continue fighting even under extremely difficult conditions, one can't say the same about the Russians. The Kursk operation has shown that Russian defenses often collapse quickly when you apply enough pressure. If Ukraine can solve its supply situation (regarding material and personnel), it may very well be able to seize even bigger parts of the Russian Federation. On the other hand, if they can't overcome their shortcomings, Russia will prevail. Like in every war, the outcome depends on many factors. We have little to no influence on the events but what everyone can do is support Ukraine in one form or the other. Giving unrealistic and false assessments of the situation, however, doesn't help anyone.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: What would happen if a homeless person walked into a military recruiters office and told them that they wanted to join the military to have a job and better life?
Answer: I served in three armies and fought in two wars, and when I pass a homeless person on a park bench, I often take a closer look at them. I’m curious about the clothes they wear (especially their trousers) and how they carry their bundle. If someone can sleep in the open during all seasons, they may know a thing or two about survival. This is certainly a quality the army can use. In general, however, the military doesn't recruit homeless people, and this is for good reason. Even here in Ukraine, where recruiters are actively on the search for draft dodgers, the homeless seem to be unaffected (I’ve never seen or heard of a homeless guy running away from the mobile TCK recruitment center teams). 95% of homeless persons in Europe (and probably elsewhere, too) are suffering from health issues that exclude them from military service. Alcoholism, drug abuse, and mental health problems are common among them. Nevertheless, there are probably a few who may make good infantry soldiers, especially the vagabond types who are constantly on the move. That the army doesn't put an effort into recruiting them is probably due to the relatively small number of such folks and the challenge of properly processing them. Someone who isn't registered anywhere, has no documents, no phone number, and no email address, is the biggest nightmare for any military administration. Without proper documents, not even the French Foreign Legion will accept you. Last but not least, the biggest hurdle in recruiting the homeless is probably their mentality. The army values punctuality, discipline, and respect for authority - qualities not typically associated with homeless people, especially the latter. Of course, I’m aware that even people who live under a roof and hold a job can be total slobs (we had some of them in our company in the German Army) but there were lousy soldiers and the army was wasting time and money with them.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: If Zelensky is such a popular hero in Ukraine why do we not see anywhere in Ukraine, even in the western part, any demonstrations of support for him and his policies?
Answer: You must live in an autocratic state or a dictatorship. Ukraine is a democracy. In democracies, pro-government demonstrations are highly unusual. If you like your president, you can show your support for him (or her) by voting for them in the next elections. If you don't like what your political leaders are doing, on the other hand, you may decide that waiting for the next elections takes too long and go to the streets. Protesting against your government without fear of retribution is a basic human right in every democracy. In Ukraine, there are constant protests against government policies. This doesn't mean that people do not agree with the way the country is run per se but they do not approve of certain policies (for example, a specific law). Often, these protests lead to changes. Unpopular draft laws are withdrawn, government officials are sacked (or not), and even army commanders have been placed under scrutiny after public protests Ukraine is under attack by Russia and it is fighting for its survival. Therefore, some civilian rights had to be limited and suspended under martial law. However, these are temporary measures, limited to a few months. The Ukrainian parliament, the Rada, constantly has to approve the continuation of these measures. Even with the war ongoing, Ukrainian citizens enjoy living in a democracy where basic human rights are guaranteed. This is one of the reasons they are fighting so hard against the Russian invaders. They don't want to live under a dictator.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Are soldiers still superstitious?
Answer: You bet they are. When I was fighting for the Croats in Bosnia, I never (re)-used the gear of our comrades who were killed in action. I always thought it brings bad luck. For the same reasons, I also never cut my hair when I was on a training course in the German Army. Once, this brought me into conflict with an instructor but I didn't care. In Ukraine, one of the first presents I received from the locals was some kind of herb with magic qualities that, according to the person I got it from, the mother of a Ukrainian soldier, “will protect you from all evils”. I'm pretty sure her son is carrying a tiny bag with the same unknown herb with him, just like I do. Probably his whole army unit has one. Maybe it doesn't work but I would never leave home with out it. At the same time, I would never go near the frontline wearing anything with a skull on it. Many combat units here have badges with skulls on their uniform but in my opinion, a skull cannot bring you good luck. And, without a lot of good luck, your life may end very soon here. I'm not even a soldier anymore but old habits die hard.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Can Zelensky spare the troops for his silly invasion? Wouldn't it be better to use them in the eastern front where Russia is advancing? Perhaps Russia deliberately encouraged this to keep opposition weak in teh Eastern front.
Answer: Although this question could certainly have been better worded, it has some valid points. Opening a new front when your forces are already overstretched and under constant pressure on a more than 1,000 kilometers long frontline is usually a very bad idea. The General staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine is not completely stupid so they knew about this. That despite the risks involved, they still decided to execute this operation may have had several reasons: Drawing enemy troops from other frontline sectors takes some pressure off from other Ukrainian units. However, this is only true if a.) you do not commit more forces than the enemy, and b.) your operation is successful and you don't get bogged down. In other words, a fast “Blitz” that forces the enemy to send a disproportionately high amount of troops to defend their turf. Until now, it seems the Ukrainians are doing the right thing but this operation is far from over. An ammunition case for an incendiary bomb that was produced by our 3D printers in Ukraine. This war is also a war of logistics and the side with the better support has an enormous advantage. The moment the Russians are able to effectively stop the Ukrainian troops and establish a new defensive line, all Ukrainisn advantages will be lost and there’ll be no military reasons to continue the operation. Other reasons to conduct such an operation are political and psychological. As long as you don't lose too many soldiers, it boosts your country’s morale and demoralizes the enemy. At the same time, controlling a decently sized piece of Russian land may become a bargaining chip in future peace negotiations. It's too soon to say whether the Ukrainian operations in Kursk and other Oblasts (administrative regions) were a smart thing to do or let to an unnecessary waste of resources. As with the Ukrainian counteroffensive in summer ’23 (which was an unmitigated disaster), we should wait a few weeks before we make an assessment. One thing, however, is already safe to say. This war, is far from over and seizing more land or more cities doesn't mean a lot. Ukraine is a big country and Russia is even bigger. Seizing a dozen of Russian (or Ukrainian) villages may enthuse some folks at home but it doesn't change a thing. It's a combination of who applies the better strategy and tactics, who will adapt faster, and who has the longer breath that will decide this war.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Will Russia declare an all-out war and fully mobilize its manpower if Ukraine invades Crimea?
Answer: Except for acting butthurt and issuing empty threads, they wouldn’t do anything. The Russian war machine reached its peak around one month ago, and we are now witnessing a slow but continuous decline in their military’s offensive capabilities. This doesn't mean that they aren't a threat anymore but at this moment, they aren’t even capable of protecting their homeland (Kursk, Bryansk, Belgorod). Declaring an “all-out war” wouldn’t help them. To “fully mobilize” their manpower, the Russians would need a lot of money. Unfortunately for them, they have less and less of it. A Ukrainian F-16 fighter jet. The first ones have already been spotted flying over Russian territory. (Picture: Efrem Lukatsky) Just like its military, Russia’s economy is slowly deteriorating. A total mobilization would only accelerate this process. In addition, the Russians have shown their complete ineptitude in properly recruiting, training, and equipping their soldiers. They don't need more people in uniform, but better ones. If the West increases its support for Ukraine (and only then) we may witness Russia’s collapse. After this, Crimea will return to Ukraine, and there will be no need to invade it.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: How often do soldiers forget how to salute properly?
Answer: Saluting is so easy and simple that you can only forget it intentionally. Usually, an improper salute is a form of disrespect. In some military units, however, giving a sloppy and incorrect salute means you’re privileged. Because of your status (not necessarily your rank), you get away with it. We had a longer-serving private in our paratrooper unit in Germany who was the only one who could give an atrociously executed salute to our captain without having all hell break loose. This private was working as the company clerk for many years and without him (and his goodwill), the company would probably have sunk into chaos. Another example was my platoon commander during NCO (Non-Commissioned Officer) school. His last name was “Spreizer” which means “spreader” (someone who is spreading something) in English. Probably because of this, he always spread his pinky finger when he was saluting. It looked ridiculous. Most often, however, soldiers “forget” to salute at all. There’s a superior coming your way and instead of saluting him, an extremely interesting grass knob on the ground is suddenly demanding all your attention. Some soldiers go even further and go completely into hiding just to avoid saluting an officer they don't like.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: How are you affected by the war going on in Ukraine?
Answer: I haven’t slept much since the Russian invasion started, that much is sure. At my age, sleeping is maybe the greatest pleasure life has to offer. As I work in Ukraine to support soldiers in the Armed Forces, I also haven’t seen many of my pre-war friends for a long time. I think these are the only negative effects. At an army base near the frontline in Donetsk. On the upside, I made a lot of new friends. People from all over the planet: Ukrainians, Poles, Brits, Canadians, South Africans, and even an Argentinian. The best thing, however, is that I can do something I like and where I’m good at. Despite the long working hours, the stress, and the (occasional) dangerous moments, I wouldn't want to change places with anyone in the world.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: In your opinion about the bold and courageous Ukrainian attack on Russia, is this a smart move to relieve pressure on the front lines and a morale blow to the Russian home front, or a stupid, suicidal move?
Answer: Whenever people ask me this question (and this happens quite a lot), I tell them: “ask me again in two weeks!” Ukraine has put a tight information lid on this operation. What we know about the Ukrainian units fighting on the territory of the Russian Federation can be summarized in one word: zero. If you don't know jacksh*t about a thing, however, it's impossible to give a (positive or negative) assessment of it. I strongly recommend everyone not to believe any information about the Kursk operation that is circulating online. This goes for all sources whether they are pro-Russian, neutral, or pro-Ukrainian. As good as all of the news (including pictures and videos) is complete crap coming from people with zero information (although, of course, they pretend otherwise). Therefore, relax, stay calm, and let the Armed Forces of Ukraine do their job. Time will tell.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: When you are at a real war. Do you think sometimes that what you do is not right?
Answer: You should never do this! These thoughts are verboten (forbidden)! First of all, doing so is completely futile. What are you going to do when, on one sunny day on the frontline, you figure out that your side are the bad guys? You can hardly go to your platoon commander and ask him to be relieved from duty. It will only lead to trouble, a lot of it. People like you are bad for morale. But even if you keep your opinions to yourself, these thoughts will make you feel miserable and depressed. In a combat situation, however, keeping your head clear of distractions is an important survival tool. You need your mind and your senses to survive this thing! Servants of evil: captured Russian soldiers in Ukraine. (Picture: Anatolii Stepinov) This is also why during downtime, the military will often keep you busy. They hate nothing more than soldiers getting bored and starting to use their brains. It's not always because your side may be the evil one but there's so much crap going on in every military that any sane and normal person would probably refuse half of the orders they get- if they had the time to think about it. On the other hand, nothing prevents you from starting to think about your time in the war when the fighting is over. Once they were out of the military, many German WWII soldiers realized that the regime they were fighting for was criminal. Of course, this realization came very late, but when you know how the army works, you can hardly blame them for it.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Why are Ukrainian soldiers buying their own weapons in order to fight the Russians in Donbas?
Answer: They usually don't do this. As it is in most other countries, the military issues you a weapon. However, there are some cases in Ukraine where soldiers bring their private weapons with them to the frontline: A privately owned shotgun on the shooting range in Ukraine. (Picture by the author of this post) What happens more often than soldiers bringing their private guns to the frontline, however, is that they acquired a second rifle from a dead or surrendered Russian soldier. You don't need two rifles, so some of them may hand over their army-issued rifle and keep using their war trophy.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Are you surprised by Ukraine's launch of an incursion into Russia's Kursk region?
Answer: I’m not surprised at all. This isn't the first time the Ukrainians have conducted an incursion into the territory of the Russian Federation and it won't be the last. These operations always tie down a lot of enemy troops which brings relief to the Ukrainian soldiers in other areas of the frontline (especially in Chasiv Yar and Pokrovsk.) As to the military situation and the scale of this operation, we all need to be patient. We should wait and not speculate. Everything will be much clearer in a week or two.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: How do I find out if a “veteran” is actually a veteran?
Answer: I recently met with two former paratroopers. We were talking about our work in Ukraine when a helicopter was flying slowly over the city. As if someone had given a secret command, we stopped talking, everyone looked in silence at the aircraft for two seconds, and then we picked up the conversation where we left it. A German Army C-160 “Transall” dropping paratroopers at the German Arbore and Air Transport school in Altenstadt, Bavaria, Germany. (Picture: German airborne museum) Paratroopers are like little children and they adore watching aircraft. When I was at NCO (non-commissioned officer) school at the German airborne school, one of our classroom instructors tried to stop us from running to the windows whenever an airplane flew over the dropzone outside. The poor officer gave up his efforts after a couple of days. I haven't seen such behavior with civilians. They either do not look at planes at all (I have no idea how they can resist the temptation), or they won't stop looking and (much worse), commenting about it.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Does the Ukrainian army still receive large numbers of international volunteers?
Answer: There are no official numbers but from what I can observe, there are still many foreigners arriving. What has changed a bit are the countries where these fighters come from. At the beginning of the war, most foreigners came from Western Europe and North America. There are still people coming from these places but most new soldiers are now from South America. There's an astonishingly high number of Columbians serving in the International Legion and other Ukrainian units. Since English language skills aren't required anymore if you want to join the Legion, hundreds of Spanish and Portuguese speakers have joined (the latter mostly from Brazil). You also meet a lot of Asians here, for example, from the Philippines. Altogether, I think the numbers of people who are coming are quite stable.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Are the figures of Russian combat losses in Ukraine accurate?
Answer: The number of Russian combat losses published by the Ukrainian authorities are pretty accurate. If you think Russia's losses are significantly lower, ask yourself the following questions: Short: Russian casualty rates are indeed that high. Russian bloggers with connections to the military have confirmed this on several occasions.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Are people that volunteered to join the Ukraine foreign legion but got rejected due to no military experience still trying to make their own way into the frontlines?
Answer: Nowadays, it’s rather uncommon that the International Legion rejects someone because they lack military experience. The Legion has its own training courses where they teach you all the things you need to know. In addition, the actual situation on the frontlines doesn't allow for the army to be too picky when it comes to setting recruiting standards. The Legion does not only reject new applicants but also kicks people out (mostly for disciplinary reasons). Other people leave voluntarily for various reasons. Two foreign volunteers, an Albanian from Kosovo and a former US Marine, who are serving in a regular Ukrainian unit on the southern frontline. The Legion is usually the first address to go for foreign volunteers but once they've been around a bit, they often meet other foreigners (from their country) who serve in other Ukrainian units and they decide to join them. Therefore, there's always a small flux of “have been” and “wanted to join but got rejected” legionnaires on the search for another outfit. These guys usually don't have a problem to find a unit. There's a brutal war going on and people who voluntarily want to go to the frontline do not exactly run around in abundance here. There are foreigners now in practically every Ukrainian combat unit. Brigades where many foreigners are serving are, for example, the Karpathian Sich brigade and the so-called Chapter. Brigade from Kharkiv.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Is it ethical and wise for Ukraine to force men ages 18-60 to stay and fight despite having no training?
Answer: Everyone gets training. Nobody in Ukraine is going to the frontline without having received the minimum skills to be able to survive on the battlefield (usually, 60 days of basic infantry training). There is room for improvements, for example, more TCCC (tactical combat casualty training) and demining techniques, but this is something the new soldiers learn once they arrived in their combat units. Some of my (civilian) friends on the shooting range. Many Ukrainians who haven't been drafted yet are already getting prepared for their (inevitable) military service. (Picture by the author of this post) Ukraine “forces to stay” young men “to fight” because it's a) their country, b) this country is under attack and c) there's compulsory military service. Under the same circumstances, every country in the world would do exactly the same. However, it's doubtful that many nations could defend their home country with the same determination and success that the Ukrainians have demonstrated.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: At the start of the Ukraine war, there were lots of spies and collaborators inside Ukraine. We never hear of them anymore. Does Russia still have a sizable group working inside Ukraine helping Russia?
Answer: There are still plenty of people spying for Russia in Ukraine. Most of them do it for the money. The Russians randomly send messages to Ukrainians where they offer payment for information (some of my colleagues received such messages, of course they didn't respond). If you want to work for the Russians, you just send them the info you have gathered (they are mainly interested in the locations of Ukrainian army bases and the effectiveness of Russia missile strikes) and they'll immediately pay you via an online payment service. A civilian woman in Donbas near the frontline. Impossible to know whether she's just curious or has ulterior motives. (Picture by the author of this post) You don't need to meet any Russian handler or physically receive money or instructions, everything is handled online. In my opinion, this system showed some results for the Russians. If you're a Ukrainian army commander and you're not careful, these spies can cause you a big headache. It's also very difficult for the Ukrainian security services (SBU) to catch them. There are still many civilians living near the frontlines and most of them are poor and desperately in need of money. How do you know whether the old man passing your army base on his bicycle is a spy or just a harmless peasant? So, yes, there are still a lot of spies here. The Russians pay relatively well and some people do not think about the consequences: getting caught as a spy for Russia will get you at least 15 years in prison.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Can an American fly to Poland and go into Ukraine without needing anything other than a passport to help volunteer?
Answer: I don't think it’s a good idea to come here without having a few things sorted out beforehand: A place where you'll work. People do not like to take someone they don't know, even for an unpaid volunteer position. So, don't be lazy. Start contacting organizations in Ukraine while you're still at home. You should have some money with you and a credit card. Life isn't very expensive but as most volunteers do not get paid and often also have to pay for their accommodation, you cannot come here with completely empty pockets. Think about the health insurance thing. What happens if you get really sick here and need to be medevaced home? With my Polish volunteer friend. He is helping the war effort from day one of the Russian full-scale invasion. If you want to join the military, you should have your military documents from your home country's army with you. There were too many liars here who said they had been Special Forces but who couldn't hit any targets on the range. This doesn't mean that you necessarily need to have all those things. I met people here who came with nothing but a bit of money and their passports and who found a good position after only a few weeks. If you think you're that good and that you don't need all these things, you may try your luck. In this case, as a bare minimum precaution, you should have at least enough money with you to buy a ticket home.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: How does your mind think/feel after you almost died?
Answer: After you almost got killed, first there's the shock. You feel numb and the fact that you're still alive somehow doesn't feel right. “Shouldn't I be dead?” The next day, however, you'll feel unexpectedly good. Shock and numbness have been replaced by happiness, sometimes even euphoria. You’re the man (or woman), you cheated death! After another day, you’ll become much calmer. This is the phase I always enjoyed the most. Things that were completely normal and mundane for you only a couple of days ago, have become pleasurable activities: a walk in the park. Smelling the flowers. A good meal. Nothing in the world can stress you out. In the veterans hospital after my last injury. The last time after I almost got killed (by a Russian artillery strikein Donetsk), I bought myself a big ice cream. Usually, I’m not eating these kinds of things but man, did I enjoy this one! It was like the first ice cream I ever tasted. Apart from the occasional flashbacks, life will return to normal pretty quickly. After a week, you won't think about your luck anymore all the time (especially if it wasn't the first time you almost died). It's rare that people become traumatized by such an experience. We are often much tougher than we think we are.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Is it possible for me to join the Ukrainian Foreign Legion even without combat experience?
Answer: I talk with many foreigners who want to join the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU). Many of them do not understand why prior field experience (although it is not required) is such a big deal with the combat units: The AFU doesn't care much about what you’ve learned in other militaries; they will teach you what they think you need to survive on the battlefield. However, having fought in other wars (i.e. having been on the receiving end of enemy fire), lowers the chances that an applicant changes their mind. This is a question of managing (scarce) resources. The AFU cannot afford to train and equip foreign volunteers who suddenly want to drop out at the last minute and go home. An ambulance near the frontline. Fighting for the Armed Forces of Ukraine is an honorable thing to do but it’s also extremely dangerous. (Picture taken by a combat medic from a unit we support) Unfortunately, many foreign volunteers who come to Ukraine are more concerned about the gear they may need and their paychecks than whether they have the right mental attitude to do the job. Fighting in Ukraine is extremely dangerous. You’ll probably get harmed physically and mentally. You may get killed. You'll see your comrades die and, let's not forget about this issue, you’ll have to kill people, often from a close distance. Don't worry about the ballistic helmet and vest, the army will give you everything you need! However, before you come here, think about your mental strength: do you have what it takes to go through “storms of steel”? War is not a video game and not a movie. It’s about killing and dying (mostly the latter). If you’re not ready, please don’t waste anyone's time here. Do not come!

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Would Ukraine be forced to surrender if Russia actually started fighting and began a nationwide mobilization of millions of men?
Answer: I’m always the first one saying we shouldn't underestimate the Russians. On the other hand, there’s no need to make them appear stronger than they are. Ukraine is suffering from the war effort but so is Russia. The Russian economy is in the sh*ts and nobody halfway sane wants to pick up a rifle for Uncle Putin and die. Saying that the Russians have not yet started “actually fighting” but somehow just make a “half-hearted” effort is, of course, idiotic. They lost tens of thousands of their soldiers only this summer (during their botched operation north of Kharkiv) and many more in Bakhmut and Avdiivka. The Russians may not be very good at it but there's no doubt that they’re fighting. Russia wants to drag Ukraine into a war of attrition where the Russians (because of their larger population and industrial base) have clear advantages. However, as long as the United States, Britain, Poland, and some other Western countries continue their support, Ukraine cannot lose this war. The West is slowly increasing ammunition and weapons production and Putin, with his only allies being North Korea and Iran, will not be able to do the same forever. In the short and mid-term, the Russians may have an advantage, but in the long term, they are no match for the West.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: How does sleeping in shifts work for soldiers on long deployments?
Answer: We slept in shifts at the frontline during the Bosnian War. Our platoon commander made a roaster that showed everyone when they were on and off guard duty. The problem was always the lack of personnel. The fewer people you have to guard a frontline sector, the less sleep you’ll get. In addition, you cannot let a guy go to his position alone. There should be at least one person with them. Another factor is that nobody can stand guard in a trench longer than three hours (two hours is ideal). You’re simply getting tired and lose focus. So, let’s say your platoon is down to nine guys (a normal occurrence after three years of fighting) and you have two positions to hold (i.e. four people have to be on guard duty at any time). Your sleep/duty roaster would look like this one: From 20:00 to 23:00 soldiers B C D E are on guard duty while soldiers F G H I sleep. (Soldier A is the platoon leader who rarely does guard duty. He has many other things to do). From 23:00 to 02:00 F G H I are on duty and B C D E sleep. It continues like this for the rest of the night. Every soldier has six hours of guard duty and six hours off time. A fixed machine gun position from my platoon in Bosnia. One also shouldn't forget that the three hours of rest also include the time it will take you to get your gear ready, walk to the position, and relieve the soldiers who were posted there. If your position is two kilometers away from your sleeping quarters (i.e. bunker), you’ll have considerably less time than three hours to rest. This sleeping/guard schedule sometimes went on for two weeks and even longer. The bunkers we slept in were sometimes extremely narrow and the roofs were leaking water when it rained. In addition, it was either too hot or too cold, people made noise, many snored, and there was always some chatter on the radio. There were also a lot of rodents. If you have a problem with mice and rats, the frontline isn't the right place for you. On many nights there were alarms or the enemy artillery pounded our positions. In other words, no sleep at all. After two weeks, everybody was a wreck.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Do you think after 2 years of brutal war in Ukraine, the West has underestimated Russia’s strength and potential?
Answer: There certainly was a lot of wishful thinking involved. In addition, there has never been a war in history where so many absolute amateurs gave their public “expertise”. There was a point in time, right after Ukraine’s successful counteroffensives in late ‘22, when many people in the West thought the thing was more or less won. Their opinions were formed by well-meaning but ignorant “experts” who were confusing their wishes (Ukraine winning fast and with minimum support from the West) with the harsh reality: a brutal war that may take several more years and that can only be won by Ukraine when the West gets far more serious about its support. In all honesty, we shouldn't forget that many real experts warned us about becoming too euphoric. As their opinions weren't popular, they either weren't heard or (even worse) were dismissed as “defeatism”. Now we are where we are. The party is over but the fighting goes on. The situation isn't hopeless, but instead of posting all these meaningless frontline videos where your side is always kicking a**, people should become more serious. It may be hard to swallow for some of us but Ukraine needs more support and less of our opinions, analyses, expertise, and advice.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Why do you block the faces of Ukrainian military personnel in pictures all the time? Is it just for OpSec to not give away where specific units are, or is it to protect the individual soldiers from possible Russian retaliation?
Answer: I take most of the pictures that I post here myself. I obscure the faces of the people in my pics for the following reasons: Last but not least it’s a trust issue. The soldiers we work with trust us. When publishing images from the frontline, one single mistake can cost a person’s life and I don't want to be the guy who made such a mistake.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Do you believe in karma? Why or why not?
Answer: During the Bosnian War, I witnessed a Croatian soldier mistreating an enemy prisoner of war. The Croat's brother had been killed in combat during the battle and when he received the bad news, his reaction was to seek revenge for his brother's death on this prisoner of war Three days later, this Croatian soldier was killed during an artillery attack. I think everyone in our unit was wondering if these two events, him committing these atrocities and his subsequent death, were somehow connected. (To their credit, not one of them approved of the deceased soldier's actions). When you're fighting a war, or (as I do now) delivering supplies to frontline troops and you see all these folks dying, you're longing for an explanation: Why did X die but I’m still alive? Can it be more than just luck? Are there hidden rules we don't know about? Did maybe his behavior lead to his demise as a sort of divine or cosmic punishment? A soldier of the Croatian Defense Council during the war in Bosnia. (Picture: Hercegovacki Portal) After having been through many of these situations, my opinion is clear: there’s no such thing as karma. It would be nice if there were, but let's not fool ourselves. Sometimes, the guy who has bad luck has been asking for it but most of the time, fate strikes completely random. There’s no pattern. Instagram videos do not represent reality. Even worse, it's often the good guys who die first. Caring about your comrade certainly is a good thing to do but in a combat situation, this can be extremely dangerous. On the other hand, the guys who only think about saving their own skin have a much better chance to survive. This may be sad but it should not keep us from living a virtuous life. If the only thing that prevents you from being a total a-hole is the fear of getting your a** kicked by karma (or God's wrath), you weren’t a good person from the very beginning. We should respect each other because it's the right thing to do. Grown-up people don't need karma tales.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: How have you handled traumatic events in your life using skills you learned from your work or hobbies?
Answer: Last May, I lost two friends during a Russian artillery attack in the Donetsk region. My Ukrainian coworker and I were only a few meters away from ground zero and we both were injured. Of course, you are shaken when something like this happens to you. However, and this is where I think many traumatized people make a mistake, we didn't retreat into a cocoon (there was no time for it anyway) but we openly spoke about the events with our friends. I think this helped a lot. We had good people that you could trust 100% and although they were more than a thousand kilometers away from the frontline (in Western Ukraine) we knew they were working day and night for us. I never had the feeling that people did not care about us or our friends who died and this was very calming and reassuring. Getting out transporter ready for the next trip. (Picture by the author of this post) In addition, after a week of getting our wounds treated, we went straight back to the place where all had happened. For me, it was extremely important, that we return to this location and that we continue our job. First, if you let such an event determine your future actions (i.e. abandon your job and your responsibilities) you may feel good for a while with your peaceful office life but these feelings won't last very long. After a couple of weeks (and this I know from my experience as a former soldier), when your emotions have cooled down and self-introspection kicks in, you’ll feel like the biggest a-hole on the planet. Another problem is that the longer you stay away from the dangerous areas, the harder it will become to get back there. When you fall off your horse, you should get right back up on it, not the next day. One of my German journalist colleagues Ukraine had an extremely traumatic time when the paratrooper unit he was embedded with got surrounded by Russian forces. For fourteen hours, he didn't know if he would get out of this hell alive. The situation got so bad that the paratroopers started to make preparations to kill themselves: nobody wanted to fall into Russian hands alive. My colleague survived and when I asked his friends how he was doing, they told me he had gone to Greece on holiday. After three months, he still hasn't returned (his parents have a house on a Greek island) and I doubt he’ll ever work as a war reporter in Ukraine again. Of course, everybody reacts differently to a traumatic event but staying active (i.e. avoiding sedentary activities), talking to good friends about it, and not shying away from the event that caused you pain works in many cases.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: What is your most terrifying war souvenir?
Answer: For me, it's terrifying because I almost had the same fate. I'm talking about my old phone. It was in my hand when a Russian artillery strike hit the house right next to me. The phone fell to the ground and I wisely decided not waste my time with looking for it. I barely got away alive (with a few scratches). Energy saving mode activated. Some Ukrainian soldiers found it the next day, more than a hundred meters away from where I lost it. One of my buddies in our office framed it and put a commemorative plaque on it. We will probably auction it off and give the proceeds to the armed forces.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Is the American-made M-2A2 Bradley infantry fighting vehicle the best infantry fighting vehicle in Russia’s war on Ukraine?
Answer: Let's compare the Bradley to the other types of Infantry Fighting Vehicles the Ukrainians are fielding,. To no one's surprise, the Russian/Soviet BMP-2s that are operated by both sides turned out to be complete failures. They are too lightly armored to survive on the Ukrainian battlefields. The performance of the BMP's 30mm autocannon is underwhelming. It is said that reloading the ammo is an extremely complicated maneuver that can take up to two hours! These vehicles also aren't mine resistant and having the fuel tanks installed in the doors where the armored infantry is supposed to mount and dismount maybe wasn't the best design idea. The German Marder has delivered a solid performance. It's heavily armored and provides good crew protection. In my opinion, its 20mm autocannon is a little bit too weak (especially in comparison with the CV-90 and the Bradley) but I haven't heard any complaints from Ukrainian soldiers yet. A Swedish CV-90 in Ukrainian service. (Picture: Kyiv Post) Both, the Swedish CV-90 and the American Bradley, are a big success in Ukraine. Their armor is about on the same level with the Marder but both vehicles have better (i.e. more powerful) cannons. The Ukrainian CV-90s have 40mm autocannons while the Bradley is equipped with the (now famous) 25mm Bushmaster cannon. On the battlefields of Ukraine, only the side with the heavier armor and the stronger weapons will survive. This means the CV-90s are clearly the best Infantry Fighting Vehicles that are used in this war.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: What are the best underrated war films?
Answer: I'm a big fan of “The Wild Geese” from 1978. You need to watch this movie with a good friend, and some cigars and a bottle of whiskey in front of you. It’s not “a” mercenary movie but “the” mercenary movie. It’s from an earlier age, so don't expect too much political correctness. Still, the dialogues are a hundred times better than in some modern mercenary flicks (“The Expendables” comes to mind). The cast includes some of Hollywood's most famous (Richard Burton, Richard Harris, Roger Moore, and Hardy Kruger) and, of course, they know how to act. The movie also has an amazing soundtrack. The theme song "Flight of the Wild Geese" was written and performed by the (equally underrated) Joan Armatrading What I like most about “The Wild Geese” is that it is a reminder of a bygone time. The mercenaries are former members of the most elite British regiments, all with combat experience, and they a more interested in the thrill than the money. Richard Harris in “The Wild Geese”. (Picture: Rank Film Distribution) Unlike our foreign volunteer fighters from today (beware of calling them mercenaries!) who won't touch a rifle before they have signed a contract with life insurance and all kinds of benefits, the mercs in this flick follow their leader Colonel Faulkner (played by Richard Burton) to the darkest places of Africa without asking any questions. It’s about comradeship and trust. The movie didn't get many positive reviews at the time of its first screening (parts of it were shot in Apartheid South Africa) but since then, people have begun to appreciate it. It’s the only watchable movie that deals with the presence of European mercenaries on the African continent during the 1950s and 60s. The story is fictional but it's clear that Daniel Carney, the author of the book the movie is based on, was inspired by the lives of mercenary commanders such as “Mad Mike” Hoare who were fighting during the Congo Wars. When I was younger and wilder, I met some of these mercenary commanders (for example, the late Charles Masy who fought with the “Kansimba Commandos” in Congo). Drinking beers with them and listening to their stories are some of my best memories. Those guys were maybe the last true adventurers, they were the real mercenaries. Nowadays, people like them do not exist anymore. This movie is a tribute to them.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: How do I dissuade my brother from joining the army?
Answer: This is a hopeless endeavor. If your brother got “the bug”, this strange feeling where young people are longing to serve in the military, there’s absolutely nothing you can do. Chain him to the radiator in the basement and he’ll find a way out of it. On the other hand, if your brother is just the average young bloke who changes his career aspirations on a daily basis, then you have nothing to worry about. His first contact with a recruiter will dissuade him. If nothing helps, letting him serve some years in the military may do him good. To be honest, it's not any of your business to meddle in other folks’ career plans, even if he's your brother.

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: How many troops can Ukraine mobilize? I am afraid that they will lose the war by attrition and not due to lack of tactics.
Answer: There are still about 3 to 5 million able-bodied men in Ukraine's recruiting pool but I don't think they'll be used to increase the size of the Armed Forces. Of course, it would be nice to have a much bigger bigger army but this would demand an extremely huge effort and it would also cost an awful lot of money. It's a bit like putting a stronger engine in your car: you gain more horsepowers but don't forget that you also need better brakes, tires, and shock absorption, and you probably have to reinforce the chassis. Your car will also consume more gas and oil. Two soldiers we support with equipment. Having to supply an army of 1.5 million instead of 1 million, is exponentially more expensive and difficult. In this case, 2+1 isn't 3 but 5 or 6. (Picture by the author of this post) What Ukraine needs instead is a constant flow of well-trained, equipped, and motivated recruits to replace their losses on the frontline. At the moment, the army needs about 20,000 new soldiers each month. If this goal can be achieved, everyone will be happy. It's better to have a smaller-sized army where everything works smoothly than a bigger one with logistics, morale, and leadership problems. Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Can a soldier really smell their enemy when fighting in a war, particularly in Vietnam?
Answer: To smell your enemy (i.e. their body odour), you need to get really close. I’ve never seen this happening and I think it’s more of a war tale than something that has happened on more than a few occassions. On the other hand, you can often detect the smells your enemy is “producing”, for example, from a campfiire, smelly food, a cigarette, deodorants, or their feces. Preparing a barbecue grill near the frontline in Ukraine. I'm pretty sure you could smell it from a long distance away. (Picture by the author of this post) Needless to say, behaviors or activities that produce a strong smell are a big no-no during missions on the frontline. There was a Vietnamese scout fighting for the French in Indochina who was said to be able to sniff out human feces from a considerable distance (more than a hundred meters, depending on wind conditions). These folks with exceptionally developed olfactory senses do indeed exist. However, I doubt they would be able to smell an enemy soldier from a longer distance. Unless the guy is an extremely smelly example of the human race, of course. Question: Is Ian Kummer an American traitor?
Answer: Talking crap about your former employer (in this case, the United States and its military) isn't treason. Question: Is Roland Bartetzko armed in Ukraine while doing this supplies and logistics job?

Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Does the Ukrainian government acknowledge that they will run out of troops before Russia does since Russia has a much larger population?
Answer: This issue is a bit more complicated. Ukraine acknowledges that is does not have enough troops (especially infantry); however, this is not because the recruiting pool has dried up. There are still between two and three and a half million able-bodied men inside Ukraine and another 600k in Western Europe. Ukraine could theoretically draft, train, and equip most of them but this would a.) cost a lot of money and b) completely ruin the economy. To get a recruit frontline ready costs about 20,000 dollars and this money has to come from somewhere. The main reason the Russians have fewer manpower problems than Ukraine is only partly due to their bigger population size: First of all, Russia doesn't care about the quality of the people they mobilize. Hard-core criminals, drug addicts, and mentally challenged people are always welcome to join. Of course, this makes for more recruits (without having to pull people away from their workplace and damaging the economy) but not for better ones. At the same time, the costs to train and mobilize these new “mobniks” are only a fraction of what Ukraine is paying. Again, lower costs mean you can recruit more people with less money. In addition, Russia often doesn't pay their soldiers’ salaries, doesn't take care of the wounded, and lets the dead ones rot on the battlefield (to avoid having to pay compensation to their families). Low quality: a destroyed Russian airborne tank. (Picture by the author of this post) The results of these two very different ways to mobilize more people for the military are seen on the battlefield: During the last two months, Russia has lost more than 1,000 soldiers every single day. Russian casualty rates are completely through the roof. At the same time, Ukraine’s casualty numbers remain low. There are no official statistics but they are under 200 troops per day. This is still too high, especially when you field quality soldiers and not cannon fodder, but because of an excellent medical system, the number is probably pretty close to a sustainable one. Furthermore, Ukraine’s casualty rates are low enough not to impact morale. Ukraine will be able to continue with its current recruiting approach for a long time. It's a careful balance between having enough money, keeping the economy going, maintaining morale, and sending enough people to the army. The Russians, on the other hand, will soon run out of expandable frontline material. Their prisons are already empty and their efforts to recruit ethnic minorities increasingly face resistance. The day the young men of Moscow and St. Petersburg will be called to the frontlines (i.e. the sons of the people who are profiting the most from Putin's war), this war will be over. These folks are only proud of their country & government as long as other people are doing the dying. When the recruiters come to knock on their doors, it will be the end of their adoration for Putin.
