Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: If you have SWAT training, could you be a decent soldier in Ukraine? Would SWAT be able to perform because of what they do?
Answer: Sure. After getting some additional training, of course. Special Weapons and Tactics teams are police and what they’re doing is very different from the missions of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU). However, in some areas, the skillsets and abilities these two organizations are teaching their members are overlapping. A SWAT team member, for example, is usually well-versed in the handling of smaller weapons such as pistols, submachine guns, rifles, and shotguns. However, I think that more important than these skillsets (which you can teach almost anyone) is the mindset of a SWAT team member. These guys volunteered for a relatively dangerous job. A former SWAT member would certainly know how to stay cool under fire. Which army in the world wouldn't want to recruit such a person? Question: What impact did the loss of the position near Krynky have on Ukraine's overall military strategy in the region?
Answer: Holding the Krynky bridgehead on the Russia-occupied side of the Dnipro River was bad for morale. Rotating the troops fighting there was extremely dangerous, you needed to cross the river in small boats. Every Ukrainian river crossing became a target for the Russian artillery. In addition, the terrain features in and near the village of Krynky did not allow for building a proper defensive line. Russian troops and artillery constantly attacked the Ukrainian bridgehead. Ukrainian soldiers during a river crossing. These kinds of operations are always risky. (Picture: Ukraine News Network) The only upside to holding Krynky was that the Russians, fearing a Ukrainian breakthrough, allocated a lot of troops to this sector. It is said that up to 40,000 Russian soldiers were facing the Ukrainian soldiers in this area. This helped to take off the pressure from other Ukrainian frontlines, especially in the Donetsk region. In the end, however, it wasn't worth it. I think Ukraine is much better off without unnecessarily risking their soldiers' lives. Holding Krynky at all costs would have led to a lot more casualties and it would also have undermined the soldiers’ morale in this frontline sector. Short: nobody in Ukraine is too sad that Krynky was abandoned. Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: How long will Ukrainian fighting capacity will be depleted by Russian tactics before the Russians simply walk to Kiev?
Answer: This question is worded terribly, but its premise is valid. Let me rephrase it: If the Russians continue with their current strategy, is there a danger of a Ukrainian defensive line collapse? The answer is a clear “no”, for the following reasons: Russia’s current tactics are to attack with small infantry groups (maximum 30 soldiers) and without heavy armor (Main Battle Tanks and Infantry Fighting Vehicles). They aim to lose as few soldiers and vehicles as possible. Furthermore, Russia conducts these attacks in many places on the frontline. They want to exhaust the already undermanned and overstretched Ukrainian defensive lines. Due to Ukraine’s lack of infantry troops, locations seized by the Russians sometimes can not be counter-attacked. As a result, the Russians momentarily gain one or two small villages every week and a few hundred square meters of ground. This doesn't seem much but it's more than what they achieved only two months ago (leaving their attack to the north of Kharkiv aside which was a total disaster for them). In the north of Kyiv after Russia’s first (failed) attempt to seize Ukraine's capital. (Picture: Hedi Aoudj) With the current pace of their advance, the Russians would reach Kyiv in around 1,000 months. Short: there is no immediate danger to Ukraine's capital. In addition, I don't see how the Russians could change their tactics to speed up their operations. They lack almost everything an army needs to conduct a successful big-scale operation: well-trained soldiers, air superiority, good logistics, and capable commanders. The only thing they have in their favor is artillery superiority but this is only regarding the quantity (of artillery pieces and ammunition) and not the quality (i.e. their accuracy and longevity). Last but not least, the more the eastern and southern frontlines retreat towards central Ukraine, the shorter the frontline (which will favor the defenders) and the longer the logistics routes for the attacker. We have witnessed many times that the further away the Russians are from their logistic hubs in the Russian Federation, the worse their combat performance. Should the Russians approach Kyiv once again, their troops will probably meet the same fate as last time: an utter and complete defeat. Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: Can you live with shrapnel in your body?
Answer: Some of my friends have problems passing through airport security scanners because of the shrapnel they caught during the war. So, yes, you can live with shrapnel in your body. After you get injured, the surgeons in the field hospitals are often too busy to take care of every little piece of metal in your body. A small piece of shrapnel from a Russian artillery strike that was taken out of my upper leg. During my first hospital stay near the frontline, the doctors couldn't take it out (it was too deep inside), so I needed to go to another hospital. I would have let it inside but the doctors wanted to do an MRI scan and you cannot do that with metal in your body. They usually leave this job to their colleagues who work in bigger and better-equipped hospitals far away from the fighting. However, if your injuries aren't too bad, you often do not even bother going there: nobody likes hospitals. If the shrapnel isn't too big, too close to a bigger blood vessel or a vital organ, and it doesn't cause any pain, many soldiers just leave it where it is. Answer: We can not rule it out. However, I don't see a way around it; Ukraine needs more military personnel. Recruiting more Ukrainian women would free up a lot of male soldiers who are serving in non-combat roles. These already trained and equipped soldiers can then be easily and quickly sent to the frontlines. The problem with foreseeing events in Ukraine is that there are too many unknown factors that influence the dynamics of this war. Question: What are the biggest lessons learned from the war in Ukraine so far from a military perspective?
Answer: After watching what is going on in Ukraine pretty closely, I think the most important lesson to draw from this war is the following: In a “hot” conventional war, there’s no room for half-measures. If you go in, you go in fully. Your country needs to mobilize all its resources and free all its potential, from day one. None of the warring factions on the battlefield (Russia, Ukraine) did this. As we all know, Russia’s planning and preparation for their invasion were abysmal. Their troops had supplies for only a couple of days and even when it became clear that this war wouldn't be over soon, it took Russia’s military apparatus many months to finally get their army into a war modus. The Ukrainian side didn’t fare better. Military planners became too optimistic after Russia’s defeats in Kharkiv and Kherson in late ‘22. The logistics to sustain a longer war were set up late and always lagged behind. Some equipment we recently sent to the frontline. Many Western organizations and NGOs (non-governmental organizations) have ceased operations in Ukraine. They didn't think the war will take so long and failed to properly plan ahead. (Picture by the author of this post) This became especially problematic with the artillery ammunition. It’s completely incomprehensible (at least for me) that nobody from the higher-ups predicted that when you shoot X number of shells every day and you have Y number in your weapons storage while Z number is produced or procured (and X is bigger than Z), there comes the day when you cannot sustain combat operations anymore. Another problem is recruiting and training. After two and a half years of fighting, the recruiting issue still isn't solved and the quality of training leaves much to be desired. All these problems have a lot to do with military leadership. Both sides suffer from old-style Soviet thinking in their ranks. It took President Zelinskyy many months to “replace” the Commander of the Joint Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Lieutenant General Yurii Sodol. Sodol screwed up so many times that he should have been court martialed a long time ago. Instead, earlier this year, they appointed him to the position of joint chief! The biggest blunders, however, were committed not by Russia or Ukraine but by Ukraine’s Western Allies. Every single piece of equipment that the West sent to Ukraine after February 24, 2022, came in insufficient quantities and too late. The NATO planners never grasped that when you have a 1,000-kilometer-long active frontline, sending Ukraine 1 million rounds of machine un ammunition is just the proverbial drop in the ocean. Of course, the German Ministry of Defense topped all this by sending 5,000 obsolete military helmets. Unfortunately, the thinking that we may somehow win this thing without giving it all we have is still in many Western analysts’ heads. This is the lesson we need to learn from this war: do not underestimate your enemy (Russia’s fault), their ability to adapt (Ukraine’s blunder) but especially do not misjudge the costs, the efforts, and the sacrifices it will take to achieve victory. Question: What would happen if Russia runs out of tanks in the war?
Answer: They could probably manage without them. Main Battle Tanks aren’t the “Kings of the Battlefield” anymore like they were in other conflicts. This has to do with several factors, for example, the mostly static character of the fighting (lack of maneuver warfare), the omnipresence of anti-tank drones, missiles (ATGMs) and loitering ammunition on the battlefield, and, of course, the abundant numbers of anti-tank mines and other obstacles. Ts doesn't mean that armor has become completely obsolete, though. Both sides heavily rely on armored personnel carriers (APCs) and infantry fighting vehicles (IFVs) to get their soldiers to and from the battleground. The more these vehicles are armored, the better they can operate. The Western-delivered IFVs on the Ukrainian side are clearly superior to their Russian counterparts. Especially the American M2 Bradleys and Swedish CV 90 have shown not only great survivability but also enough fighting power to battle even the latest Russian Main Battle Tank (MBT) models. This is where I see problems for the Russian military in the future. Compared to the West, the Russian tank design philosophy has always preferred relatively lighter and smaller tanks and armored vehicles. Question: What is the closest call you have ever had with death?

On the other hand, once the weather clears or you're in the open where your distance to the target grows to more than 50 meters (150 feet), a pistol becomes pretty useless. Sergeant First Class Leroy Petry from the US Army Rangers. After he lost his right arm during combat in Afghanistan, he used his remaining hand to apply a tourniquet and stop the bleeding. So, don't waste your breath telling an injured comrade (fatally wounded or not) things that aren’t helpful. Question: Would a one (1)-man crewed tank be feasible, and would it be more effective than a 3-4 person crewed tank?

The same goes for many other tasks that a tank crew has to accomplish: changing the tracks and cleaning the main cannon require more than one person. Of course, one could somehow automate this procedure but this would add a lot of additional weight to the vehicle. A tank crew member, on the other hand, is versatile and can do many different tasks. Where I see the main problem, however, is with problem-solving. Tanks break down all the time and get damaged, not only by enemy fire. What do you do when, during a firefight, you lose your radio communication or your hydraulics? The latter happened to us many times in training. In this case, we had two options: fix the problem or go manual (all vital systems of a tank can also be operated manually, with pedals and cranks). Good luck doing this without a second crew member! (Picture by the author of this post) Your most important task is to shoot the enemy (tank) before they can shoot you. You need to be very fast and accurate. Of course, this can be automated but four eyes will always see more than two. The traditional commander/gunner team is a proven concept and highly superior to tanks where only one person conducts the fight. Last but not least, when the sh*t hits the fan, you want to have a human being next to you who pulls your wounded a** out of the burning tank and gives you first aid. Question: How does the military handle soldiers who pretend to be sick to escape stressful, tough and/or dangerous duties?
Answer: It’s up to your commander to decide if and how sick you are. A soldier is usually allowed to see a doctor but the medical professional’s diagnosis and prescribed therapy only serve as a recommendation. In most armies, especially the ones at war, an upset stomach or a mild flu won't get you off the hook. When I was in the German Army, we used to say that as long as it doesn't bleed and no bone is broken, you're healthy enough to do your duty. In addition, with our modern medical diagnostics methods, soldiers who just pretend to be sick usually don't get away with it. However, letting military commanders overrule medical findings can lead to severe consequences: One of my friends who was serving in the International Legion for the Defense of Ukraine suffered a TBI (traumatic brain injury) from artillery fire. He went to the doctor who strongly recommended that he doesn’t participate in any combat mission at least for several weeks. His commander needed every man and because our man had no visible injuries, he was ordered to go back into battle. A few hours later, he was knocked over by the blast of an exploding Russian artillery shell for the second time. Brain scan of a US soldier who suffered a blast-related mild brain injury. The arrows point to scars that stem from lesions. These scars were visible in the brain scans of half of the US military personnel who suffered from mild TBI. (Picture: Walter Reed National Military Medical Center) Our brain can easily deal with one concussion, but sustaining a second one while you’re still recovering from the first is extremely dangerous. As a result, my friend’s brain got severely damaged (he showed me the brain scans and you didn't need to be an expert to see the big dent on the left hemisphere). He had to retire from the army for medical reasons. This is not an isolated case, but you hear similar accounts from many armies and conflicts. Even years after the war is over, former soldiers often have to fight for the recognition of their war related medical problems. To name an example, our societies had to learn about their soldiers getting sick from being exposed to toxic substances. There were the Iraqi burn pits, depleted uranium ammunition from the Yugoslav wars, or the infamous “Agent Orange” from Vietnam. So, how does the military handle the issue of soldiers who pretend to be sick? Rather badly. Question: Has Roland Bartetzko read Dave Grossman's controversial book On Killing? If so, what was the reaction?
Answer: I've read it. On Killing is a must-read for former, active, and future combat soldiers. It details what happens on the battlefield. Not the tactics, but the psychological side: the stress, the fears, and all the feelings you’ll go through before, during, and after your mission. The book doesn't stop there, it explains why something happens. For example, the euphoria many combat soldiers experience right after they’ve killed an enemy soldier and the feelings of remorse, guilt, and shame that (may) come later. This is the core of Grossman’s work. As a former combat soldier, I know what happened to me but not why. Why, for example, does one soldier come out of the hardest battle without the slightest psychological problem but his buddy (who pretty much experienced the same things) is scarred for the rest of his life? With Dave Grossman (Lt. Col. US Army Rangers, ret.) in Kyiv. Why do some soldiers freeze when they should pull the trigger? What can family members and society do to support soldiers who are returning from the battlefield? Grossman interviewed hundreds of combat veterans from different conflicts for this work but mostly from Vietnam. Their (often harrowing) accounts from the war zones are as much educating as they are fascinating. This is one of the few books that one of your comrades may read during downtime at your base and then say: “Listen to this guys, you must absolutely hear this!” On Killing has become a classic. It treats many more aspects of “The Psychological Cost of Learning to Kill in War and Society” (so it’s subtitle) but for me, the most important side of it was that it explained so many of the things I’ve experienced on the battlefield.

Chances that any reinforcements get there in time are often slim so you really have nothing to gain from attacking. That both sides come to the same conclusion and not fight isn't uncommon. Especially if combat troops are tired, low on ammunition, and at the very end of their several days-long patrol, they'll be less inclined to engage than at the beginning. Question: How were you affected by your time in combat?

Even after more than 20 years, I still compare many things that happen in my life to my time on the battlefields: “This was worse than in combat”, “I never had less sleep since I was in combat”, and so on. When you fought in a tough and brutal battle and came out of it alive and okay with yourself (i.e. you didn't freeze or run away), your combat experience will become a source of strength for you. You’ll confront future hardships and stressful situations in your life with a different attitude: “If I was able to get through all this sh*t in the war, I’ll surely master this problem!” Somewhere in the Donetsk region during a supply trip. On the other hand, if you got badly wounded, were unable to cope with the horrors of war, or became a disappointment for your peers and yourself, your time on the battlefield may cause you lifelong trauma. I was lucky. I was wounded several times but never too badly. I went through many hardships and witnessed a lot of brutalities, but there were always some friends and comrades who shared the same experiences and we always supported each other. Now that I’m in Ukraine, my former combat experience is of utmost importance. I was surprised by how easy it was for me to get used (again) to life on the front lines. Although I’m working now in a logistics and supporting role and not as a fighter, there is a constant threat of drone, artillery, and air attacks. My combat experiences not only prepared me for this extremely hostile environment but also gave me the necessary confidence: “It can't get much worse than on that sunny day in Mostar during the Bosnian War when you were lying on that asphalt road and men were getting killed left, right, behind, and in front of you.” If you want to help me support Ukrainian volunteers (civilian and military, foreigners and locals), please use the contact email in my profile description.

Question: Should every soldier have a sidearm?
Answer: There’s no need for it. Usually, only machine gunners and snipers carry a secondary firearm. You never know what will happen. Now imagine doing all these little errands with a machine gun or sniper rifle. Machine guns are big and heavy while sniper rifles are usually longer and far less compact than a standard infantry rifle. You don't want to drink your morning coffee with a German MG3 in your lap. Sniper rifles are also a bit delicate (mainly because of the optics). You should avoid exposing them to unnecessary shocks, for example, a fall to the ground. The rifle is the soldier’s bride. You carry it with you anytime and anywhere. A CZ 806 Bren 2 of the International Legion for the Defense of Ukraine. (Picture by the author of this post) Furthermore, machine guns are often used as squad weapons. They are left in a fixed position at the frontline (for example, in a trench) and aren't moved. Whoever is manning the trench is the one who will operate the machine gun. Last but not least, sniper rifles and machine guns are ill-suited for close-distance combat. When your position is overrun, you need a weapon that can quickly be aimed. All of this doesn't count for a standard infantry rifle. You can carry an M4 or a Kalashnikov with you all the time. (A rifle also gives you something to hold on to when you’re in a squatting potion behind that tree. You can put a roll of toilet paper over the muzzle). At the beginning of the war, the Armed Forces of Ukraine had been quite generous when it came to issuing secondary weapons to their soldiers (usually a pistol). This has changed. They have realized that for most soldiers, including officers, backup weapons are not necessary. You can now buy very good Picatinny rails for Kalashnikov rifles that allow you to attach all kinds of stuff. A good rifle scope also solves the accuracy issue. El Salvador, for example, has an average monthly salary of 356 US dollars. A soldier in the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) gets around 3,000 US dollars (including combat pay). The readiness to stay in Ukraine for a long time has become an important factor. In the end, it’s much better to have a South American with a military background here who came for the money than some European or US-American adventure tourists who go home after a few months. Question: Are improvised explosive devices used in the military?
Answer: Improvised Explosive Devices (IEDs) are the weapon of choice for guerrilla armies and special operations forces. Modifying an artillery shell, for example, and turning it into a booby trap does not only require special skills but it’s also not free of risks. Therefore, conventional armies hesitate to train their soldiers in the art of IED manufacturing. In addition, some Western armies consider that the use of IEDs violates international conventions. However, despite these hesitations, desperate times sometimes require desperate measures. A workshop near the frontline where improvised bombs, grenades, and mines are manufactured. I visited this location and support the soldiers that are working there with equipment. (Picture taken by one of my friends) In Ukraine, many regular units now manufacture their own booby traps. On the zero line (the line closest to the enemy) you can find hundreds of different kinds of IEDs that are not only used against enemy infantry and tanks but also against drones. At the same time, Ukrainian soldiers learn how to neutralize the explosive traps the enemy has set up. One of my friends from Germany is running such a IEDD (IED disposal) training course. A soldier in Ukraine is working on a IED during a training course. (Picture: X-Intelligence GmbH, with friendly permission) The current lack of ammunition on the Ukrainian side has accelerated these developments. While in earlier stages of the war, abandoned enemy ammunition depots had been more or less ignored by frontline troops, they now bring the ordnance to workshops near the frontline where the ammunition gets “recycled”: The primers, for example, are removed and used to make detonators (for FPV drones) while the explosive (usually TNT) is carefully melted and reused in a variety of explosive devices. These improvised workshops play an important role in Ukraine’s defense efforts. They help to compensate for the lack of ammunition supplies from the West. Question: Is the uncomfortable truth that only western troops on the ground in Ukraine can break the deadlock & achieve a major breakthrough against Russia, as despite aid, Ukraine does not have the numbers of troops to put into battle?
Answer: It’s a bit more complex than that. Ukraine does not lack the manpower to achieve a major battlefield victory per se. However, due to the current lack of sophisticated weapons and artillery ammunition, the country is fighting the war in a way that requires large numbers of troops. In addition, because of financial constraints, Ukraine cannot mobilize new soldiers in a sufficient number. Several factors come into play here: The less sophisticated your weaponry, the more troops you need and vice versa. The introduction of Western Main Battle Tanks and Infantry Fighting Vehicles on the Ukrainian battlefield has demonstrated that with modern armor, many lives can be saved. We have observed that brigades that operate Leopards, Marders, or Bradleys “consume” less soldiers than the ones that still use the old T-64s and BMPs. In addition, modern long range artillery, missile artillery, and cruise missiles can do an effective job without putting your soldiers lives at risk. More of these weapons means less bloodshed for Ukraine. In this regard, air superiority is an especially effective way to control the battlefield without sending a lot of troops into harms way. During a training with the heavy tank battalion of a mechanized brigade. (Picture by the author of this post) To make the current situation worse, the lack of artillery ammunition leads to an extremely “personnel intensive” kind of warfare. If you have no artillery to keep your enemy at bay (and also lack air superiority), you need to use the other means that are left at your disposal, for example, the infantry. Ukraine still has enough able-bodied male citizens that can be mobilized but recruiting, training, equipping, and paying them costs a lot of money. Increasing the number of recruits also negatively affects the economy. The solution to these problems is simple: If we give Ukraine more and better weapons (Taurus cruise missiles, F-16s, etc.) and, at the same time deliver millions of artillery shells, they’ll need less troops to defend their territory. And if we give them additional financial aid, they’ll be able to recruit more people without completely ruining their economy. Question: Does combat training realistically prepare soldiers for the psychological devastation of war?
Answer: Most instructors in Western armies have zero or only limited combat experience. Of course, it's impossible to convey something you do not possess. But even in cases where you have people with extensive combat experience (for example, in Special Operations Forces), preparing soldiers for the psychological effects of warfare is a tricky task. One of my friends, a British volunteer, on the frontline in Donetsk last year. All you can do is tell them about your experiences, make the training as realistic as possible, and, most importantly, be honest with your people: Combat is worse than everything they’ll ever experience. It will have a lasting effect on their lives and not a positive one. One moment, everything is fine and just a split-second later, all hell breaks loose. You can die at any moment. Still, if conducted by good instructors, combat training can give soldiers an idea about what to expect. Of course, it cannot teach them everything about what the fighting will do to their minds, but it can make them aware of the kind of ordeal they may go through. Question: Lets say Putin takes Kiev, then what. Is he intending to keep soldiers stationed in Ukraine for years to come in hopes of people forgetting about the invasion?
Answer: It may sound cynical, but from a purely cost/benefit point of view, the Russians taking Kyiv and occupying Ukraine would be a dream come true for the West. The biggest land war in Europe since World War II would suddenly turn into the biggest guerrilla war ever. Of course, this would lead to even more suffering and destroy Ukraine, but on the other hand, the West would need to invest only a fraction of what we are giving to Ukraine at the moment. Maximum ROI (return on investment): the successful guerrilla war against the Soviet occupation in Afghanistan cost the American taxpayers roughly twenty billion dollars. In comparison, the (lost) war against the Taliban cost them more than a trillion. Guerrilla campaigns are the cheapest form of warfare. A Russian occupation of Ukraine and the ensuing insurgency would bleed the Russians out, economically as well as morally, for many years to come. I think the Russians have understood this now (they certainly didn’t at the beginning of their failed invasion). There will probably be some pro-Russians pointing out that “Russia never intended to take all of Ukraine,” but this, of course, is not accurate. Question: Why doesn't NATO say "enough is enough" and send in troops to Ukraine?
Answer: We should quickly forget any proposal regarding the deployment of Western troops, either from individual countries or under NATO command, to Ukraine. This will never happen. Not so much because it would lead to a further escalation of the war and the heightened risk that the fighting spreads into other countries, but because of the following: There’s zero, and I repeat, zero willingness from any Western country to send its soldiers to Ukraine. There was this recent proposal that Western troops may, for example, guard the Ukrainian side of the border to Belarus and so free thousands of Ukrainian soldiers from this duty, but this is a nonsense idea. Everything the West has sent to Ukraine has become a preferred (albeit difficult to hit) target for the Russians: the Leopard and Abrams tanks, for example, but especially the HIMARS. If there’s a Leopard 2 on the battlefield, the Russians do everything they can to destroy it. They may sacrifice a lot of men and material to attain this goal but the propaganda victory is deemed more valuable than the lives of a few dozen soldiers. We would see a similar Russian reaction if the West puts boots on the ground, even if it happens far away from the frontline. These troops would immediately become the target of Russian drones, missiles, and special operations forces teams. A German Leopard 2 tank on the Eastern frontline. (Picture: AFU) Another problem is how to send a combat unit without a valid legal mandate (for example, a UN Resolution) to a country at war. Most constitutions of democratic countries forbid such actions. In addition, in most Western countries such high risk missions are voluntary based: soldiers from different units volunteer and new deployment units are formed. These “battle groups” often lack cohesion and unified training. They are good enough for peacekeeping or low intensity warfare missions but not for a “hot” conventional war. Last but not least, sending these troops would require a massive logistical effort. Weapons, vehicles, and ammunition must be brought to Ukraine. Due to the lack of appropriate infrastructure, such an operation would further hamper Ukraine’s own logistics. Less weapons and ammunition would get to the frontline. And let’s not talk about the costs. In countries where many people are already complaining about the high cost of this war, another huge financial burden on the nation’s budget would be difficult to sell. Short: the whole thing sounds good in theory and certainly has its value as a (rhetorical) mean to challenge the Russians, but its realization is impossible.
